Description: is an open chemical information resource maintained by the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH). Its main purpose is to provide a comprehensive public repository of chemical structures, identifiers, physicochemical properties, and biological activity data aggregated from many contributors, including screening programs and the scientific literature. PubChem is among the largest open chemical registries, hosting on the order of $10^8$ substance records and extensive links between compounds, bioassays, publications, and external databases. It is widely used for cheminformatics, data integration, and as a starting point for building compound collections for modeling. PubChem offers flexible search functionality, including text-based queries (names, identifiers), structure-based search (exact match, similarity, substructure), and batch/programmatic access via web services. These capabilities make it suitable for both interactive exploration and large-scale dataset construction, for example when mapping identifiers across resources or retrieving standardized structures for downstream analysis.

(Chemical Entities of Biological Interest) is an open-access, manually curated database and ontology of biologically relevant chemical entities maintained by EMBL--EBI~\cite{malik2025chebi}. It provides standardized chemical structures and annotations, including names, molecular formulas, charges, SMILES, InChI, and InChIKey, together with cross-references and ontology-based classifications. ChEBI contains more than 195,000 chemical entities and supports bulk data download, including structure data in SDF format, making it a useful resource for chemical data integration, annotation, and standardization.

is an open bioactivity database maintained by the European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL--EBI, United Kingdom). Its core goal is to provide curated relationships between small molecules and biological targets, with standardized bioactivity measurements (e.g., IC$_{50}$, K$_i$, EC$_{50}$) extracted and harmonized from the scientific literature. Compared with broad chemical registries, ChEMBL emphasizes quality control and consistent annotation of assays, targets, and mechanism-related metadata, which makes it especially valuable for quantitative structure--activity relationship modeling and target-based drug discovery research. ChEMBL supports text and identifier search, structure and substructure queries, and target-centric navigation (from proteins to ligands and activities). It also provides bulk downloads and an application programming interface, enabling reproducible extraction of compound--target activity datasets for machine learning, benchmarking, and method development.

is a large-scale chemical structure cross-referencing database developed and maintained by EMBL-EBI. Rather than serving as a primary repository of molecular properties, UniChem integrates identifiers from more than 40 chemical databases and establishes links between records that correspond to the same chemical structure. It includes links to major resources such as ChEMBL, ChEBI, and SureChEMBL, as well as databases in which small molecules constitute only part of the stored information. Molecules are matched primarily using standardized chemical structures and structure-derived identifiers, enabling users to map compound identifiers across otherwise independent databases. UniChem can be accessed through a web interface and REST web services, making it particularly useful for automated data integration, identifier normalization, and the aggregation of complementary chemical and biological information from multiple sources.

is a large commercial molecular database and online drug-discovery platform focused primarily on purchasable small molecules for virtual screening and compound sourcing. The database aggregates catalogs from numerous chemical suppliers and, as of August 2026, its freely downloadable full collection contains more than 140 million compounds, provided as 2D structures in SMILES and SDF formats together with unique Mcule identifiers. Molecular structures are processed using Mcule Advanced Curation (MAC), which applies more than 80 structural validation, standardization, preparation, and correction steps to reduce erroneous or poorly represented compounds. In addition to the complete collection, Mcule provides specialized subsets such as in-stock compounds and purchasable building blocks, while its web platform integrates the database with cheminformatics and molecular-modeling tools for similarity and substructure searches, property filtering, diversity selection, and molecular docking. Because it represents a large and comparatively unrestricted collection of commercially accessible chemical structures, Mcule is also useful as a source of chemically diverse and practically synthesizable molecules for large-scale molecular machine-learning datasets and pretraining applications.

is a large-scale, curated molecular dataset developed specifically for pretraining and evaluating machine-learning models in chemoinformatics. It contains approximately 222 million compounds collected from six major chemical resources—PubChem, UniChem, Mcule, ChemSpace, SuperNatural3, and COCONUT—and processed using a unified automated curation pipeline. Molecular structures are standardized and represented as canonical SMILES, while the original source and compound identifiers are retained to provide traceability to the underlying databases. The dataset combines molecules from both general chemical repositories and more specialized collections, including commercially available compounds and natural products, which gives it substantially broader chemical diversity than many commonly used molecular pretraining datasets. MolPILE was designed as a standardized, reproducible resource for large-scale molecular representation learning and foundation-model pretraining, and experiments reported by its authors show that training existing molecular models on MolPILE can improve their generalization to downstream tasks. Chemicals Database is a public regulatory information system maintained by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA, European Union; headquartered in Finland). Its primary purpose is transparency and compliance support under EU chemicals legislation, especially REACH (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals) and CLP (Classification, Labelling and Packaging). The database publishes substance identity information and, for many substances, summaries of physicochemical, toxicological, and ecotoxicological data submitted by registrants, together with hazard classifications and regulatory status (e.g., restrictions or authorisation). Search is mainly identifier- and regulation-driven: users can query by substance name, CAS/EC number and explore hazard classifications, dossier summaries, and uses/exposure information where available. For dataset work, ECHA is particularly valuable as an authoritative source of regulatory labels and hazard endpoints, although completeness and public detail vary across substances and submission types.

is an open mass spectral reference database developed through international academic collaboration (originating from initiatives in Japan and expanded globally). Its main goal is to support small-molecule identification in analytical chemistry by providing experimentally measured mass spectra, typically MS/MS spectra, linked to chemical structures and rich metadata (instrument type, ionization mode, collision energy, and acquisition conditions). Unlike structure registries, MassBank's central asset is reference spectra that enable spectral library matching and improved confidence in compound annotation. MassBank provides search by compound metadata and identifiers, as well as spectrum-oriented retrieval such as mass-to-charge (m/z) and peak-based queries, with filters for acquisition parameters. These functions make it a key resource for metabolomics and environmental screening workflows, where reference spectra are required for confirmation and for evaluating computational methods in spectrum matching and annotation.

is a free public database of commercially available chemical compounds developed at the University of California, San Francisco. Its primary purpose is to provide purchasable small molecules prepared in computationally ready formats for virtual screening and molecular docking. Unlike general chemical registries, ZINC focuses on drug-like, lead-like, and fragment-like compounds that can be readily obtained from vendors. The database contains hundreds of millions of molecules, including enumerated chemical libraries, with subsets tailored to specific physicochemical criteria. ZINC supports search by ZINC identifier, SMILES, InChIKey, and physicochemical filters (e.g., molecular weight, logP), as well as substructure and similarity queries. It also provides downloadable subsets and three-dimensional conformations suitable for structure-based drug design workflows, making it widely used in computational drug discovery and generative modeling studies.

is a free chemical structure database operated by the Royal Society of Chemistry (United Kingdom). It aggregates chemical structures and associated information from numerous data sources, providing a centralized platform for identifier mapping and cross-referencing. ChemSpider contains tens of millions of chemical entries and links compounds to external databases, literature references, spectra, and vendor information. ChemSpider offers text-based search (names, CAS numbers), structure and substructure search, and similarity queries through an interactive interface. Its strength lies in integration and cross-linking rather than deep bioactivity annotation, making it useful for resolving chemical identity and connecting heterogeneous data sources.

(COlleCtion of Open NatUral prodUcTs) is an open database dedicated to natural products and maintained by an international academic community. Its main goal is to aggregate, standardize, and curate openly available natural product structures together with associated metadata such as names, taxonomic source information, literature references, and provenance across contributing resources. Unlike broad chemical registries, COCONUT is specifically focused on the chemical space of natural products and has become one of the key open infrastructures for natural-product-based cheminformatics and molecular discovery. The resource supports search by molecular identifiers, names, and chemical structure, and provides bulk downloads in machine-readable formats for downstream analysis. Recent updates have substantially expanded its scope and improved curation workflows, provenance tracking, organism annotations, and community contribution mechanisms.

, produced by the Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS, United States), is a commercial chemical information platform widely used in academia and industry. It is built upon the CAS Registry, one of the most comprehensive curated chemical substance collections in the world, containing over one hundred million unique substances. SciFinder integrates chemical structures, reactions, properties, patents, and literature references into a unified searchable environment. Search capabilities include text queries, advanced structure and reaction search, citation tracking, and filtering by properties or document types. Although access requires subscription, SciFinder is considered a gold standard for authoritative chemical information and comprehensive literature coverage.

is a curated database developed in Canada that combines detailed drug data with comprehensive information on drug targets, mechanisms of action, interactions, and pharmacological properties. It contains thousands of approved, experimental, and investigational drugs, integrating chemical structure information with biological and clinical annotations. DrugBank bridges chemistry and pharmacology by linking small molecules to proteins, pathways, and therapeutic indications. The platform supports search by drug name, structure, target, and disease indication, and provides downloadable datasets for academic use. It is particularly valuable for translational research, drug repurposing studies, and integration of chemical data with biomedical knowledge.

is an open-access database of experimentally measured protein--ligand binding affinities, maintained in the United States. It focuses on quantitative interaction data such as K$_d$, K$_i$, and IC$_{50}$ values extracted from the literature and deposited by researchers. BindingDB contains millions of binding measurements covering a broad range of protein targets and small molecules. Users can search by compound, protein target, affinity range, or structure, and download curated activity datasets for modeling purposes. BindingDB is frequently used for benchmarking scoring functions, training affinity prediction models, and studying structure--activity relationships.

(Therapeutic Target Database) is a curated resource developed in China that provides information on therapeutic protein and nucleic acid targets, associated drugs, and corresponding diseases. Its main objective is to facilitate target identification and validation by linking molecular targets with approved and experimental therapeutics. TTD integrates chemical structures of drugs with biological target annotations and clinical relevance. Search functionality includes queries by target name, drug, or disease, with navigation between related therapeutic entities. TTD is especially useful for mapping drug--target networks and supporting systems pharmacology and drug discovery research.

Commercial chemical databases constitute a class of proprietary information systems developed by specialized organizations such as Chemical Abstracts Service, Elsevier, and Clarivate, and include platforms such as SciFinder, Reaxys, GOSTAR, Cortellis, and Derwent Innovation. These systems integrate curated chemical structures, reactions, bioactivity data, patents, and scientific literature into unified, highly structured environments designed for professional use in academia and industry. Compared with open databases, commercial platforms typically emphasize data curation quality, standardized annotation, and comprehensive coverage, particularly in areas such as synthetic pathways, medicinal chemistry, and intellectual property. They provide advanced search capabilities, including structure, reaction, and semantic queries, as well as analytical tools for drug discovery and competitive intelligence. However, access is restricted by subscription, limiting reproducibility and large-scale data extraction for machine learning applications, and creating barriers to open scientific workflows despite their status as authoritative sources of chemical information.

Chemicals Dashboard, developed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, is an open-access platform designed to integrate curated chemical identity information with data relevant to environmental chemistry and toxicology. It provides standardized chemical structures, identifiers, physicochemical properties, bioactivity data, exposure information, and links to regulatory resources. The system is built upon the DSSTox database, which ensures high-quality structure curation and consistent mapping between chemical names and structures. As described by Williams et al.~\cite{williams2017comptox}, the Dashboard was created to improve transparency, accessibility, and interoperability of chemical data used in environmental risk assessment and computational toxicology. It supports advanced search functions, batch queries, and data downloads, making it suitable for large-scale cheminformatics and machine learning applications. By integrating diverse datasets within a unified framework, the CompTox Chemicals Dashboard serves as a central infrastructure for chemical prioritization, hazard evaluation, and predictive modeling. is a large, community-curated collection of suspect chemical datasets developed within the NORMAN Network (EU environmental network). It is implemented through the NORMAN Suspect List Exchange (environmental database platform), launched in 2015 to support collaboration in high-resolution mass spectrometry screening. The Network provides scientific coordination, while the Exchange platform enables researchers and environmental agencies to share and harmonize curated suspect lists. As of 2026, the collection includes about 134 individual suspect lists comprising more than 120,550 unique chemical substances. Major categories cover pharmaceuticals, pesticides, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), industrial chemicals, biocides, transformation products, natural toxins, and other emerging contaminants. The main goal of the initiative is to improve early identification and prioritization of environmental contaminants and to promote open, harmonized chemical data exchange. The datasets are further integrated into the NORMAN SusDat database and connected with international resources such as PubChem and the US EPA CompTox Chemicals Dashboard.

is an open data science platform that hosts community-contributed datasets and machine learning competitions, including numerous chemistry-related collections. Although it is not a primary chemical registry, Kaggle provides ready-to-use datasets for quantitative structure--activity relationship (QSAR) modeling, toxicity prediction, molecular property estimation, drug discovery tasks, and materials informatics. Many of these datasets are derived from public sources such as PubChem, ChEMBL, regulatory databases, or published benchmarks, but are reformatted into machine learning--friendly structures (typically CSV files with SMILES strings, descriptors, and target labels). Kaggle’s main goal is to facilitate data-driven research and benchmarking rather than long-term curation of chemical knowledge. It supports search by keywords, tags, competitions, and domains, and provides integrated notebooks for reproducible workflows. While highly practical for rapid experimentation and model comparison, dataset provenance and standardization may vary across contributions, and users must verify data sources and preprocessing procedures before research use.

is an open-access research data repository developed by CERN and operated under the European OpenAIRE initiative. Its primary purpose is to enable researchers to share, preserve, and cite a wide range of research outputs, including datasets, software, publications, and supplementary materials. Unlike domain-specific chemical databases, Zenodo is a general-purpose repository that supports all scientific disciplines, including chemistry and cheminformatics. Zenodo allows users to upload datasets in arbitrary formats, assign persistent digital object identifiers (DOIs), and provide rich metadata describing the contents, methodology, and provenance of the data. It supports versioning, open licensing, and long-term preservation, making it particularly suitable for publishing datasets associated with scientific articles or machine learning benchmarks. In chemical research, Zenodo is commonly used to distribute curated datasets, model inputs and outputs, and reproducible workflows.

is a curated benchmark collection designed to standardize evaluation in molecular machine learning. Introduced as a unified framework for comparing predictive models, it aggregates a diverse set of publicly available datasets covering quantum chemistry, physical chemistry, biophysics, and toxicity prediction tasks. Rather than generating new experimental data, MoleculeNet harmonizes existing datasets (e.g., QM9, ESOL, Tox21, PDBbind) into consistent formats with predefined training, validation, and test splits, including chemically meaningful scaffold splits for realistic generalization assessment. The main goal of MoleculeNet is to improve reproducibility and comparability in cheminformatics and drug discovery research. It provides structured molecular representations (commonly SMILES-based) and standardized evaluation protocols, enabling fair benchmarking of graph neural networks and other machine learning methods. As a result, MoleculeNet has become a widely adopted reference framework for molecular property prediction and quantitative structure--activity relationship modeling. The

(Generated DataBase) series is a collection of systematically enumerated virtual chemical libraries developed at the University of Bern, Switzerland. Its primary objective is to exhaustively map the chemical space of small organic molecules by enumerating all possible structures satisfying defined constitutional constraints, such as atom count, valence rules, chemical stability, and synthetic feasibility filters. Unlike curated databases that compile experimentally known compounds, the GDB databases represent theoretically accessible chemical space, providing a reference for assessing the coverage of existing compound collections and for guiding exploration toward novel molecular scaffolds. The GDB datasets are distributed as downloadable files containing SMILES representations and are available in subsets filtered by physicochemical properties. These resources have been widely used in cheminformatics research for analyzing chemical space topology, training and benchmarking generative molecular design models, and identifying underexplored regions of synthetically accessible space. Due to their systematic and unbiased construction, the GDB databases serve as a foundational reference for studies requiring exhaustive enumeration rather than empirical sampling of small-molecule chemical space.

Supplementary materials associated with scientific publications were considered an additional source of chemical datasets. Relevant files were identified by inspecting the supplementary information provided on journal and publisher webpages for publications found during the literature search. These materials were typically accessible from the article landing page through sections labeled `Supplementary Information'', `Supporting Information'', `Electronic Supplementary Material'', or `Additional Files''. When supplementary data were deposited in an external repository, the corresponding repository link provided by the publication was followed. The search was not restricted to a predefined list of journals. Instead, supplementary materials were examined for relevant publications in chemistry, cheminformatics, computational chemistry, molecular machine learning, and drug discovery. Structured machine-readable files, including CSV, TSV, SDF, and TXT files, were considered when they contained identifiable chemical compounds, molecular structures, biomolecules, or measured or calculated chemical properties. Priority was given to datasets containing molecular identifiers such as chemical names, molecular formulas, SMILES. Supplementary datasets were identified using queries such as ``SMILES dataset'', ``molecular dataset CSV'', ``chemical compounds dataset'', ``SMILES supplementary information'', ``molecular dataset supporting information'', and ``chemical properties dataset''. For specific publications or datasets, the dataset or method name was additionally combined with terms such as ``supplementary'', ``supporting information'', ``dataset'', ``CSV'', ``SDF'', or ``SMILES''. For example, queries such as ``aqueous solubility SMILES dataset CSV'' and ``molecular toxicity dataset SMILES supplementary information'' were used to identify datasets containing molecular structures together with experimentally measured or annotated properties. Files were excluded when they were unavailable, unrelated to the scope of the review, insufficiently described, or provided only in an unstructured format that did not allow reliable extraction of molecular records.
